Title: GEGLU-Transformer for IMU-to-EMG Estimation with Few-Shot Adaptation
Text:
GEGLU-Transformer for IMU-to-EMG Estimation
with Few-Shot Adaptation
1st Miroljub Mihailovic, 2nd Luca Tonin, 3rd Emanuele Menegatti, 4th Stefano Tortora
Abstract—Reliable estimation of neuromuscular activation is
a key enabler for adaptive and personalized control in wearable
robotics. However, surface electromyography (EMG) remains
difficult to deploy robustly outside laboratory settings due to
electrode sensitivity, signal non-stationarity, and strong subject
dependence. In this work, we propose an adaptive IMU-to-
EMG learning framework that reconstructs continuous muscle
activation envelopes from wearable inertial measurements across
heterogeneous movement conditions. The approach combines
a Transformer encoder with Gaussian Error Gated Linear
Units (GEGLU-Transformer) to enhance cross-subject general-
ization and enable rapid subject-specific personalization. Un-
der a strict leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocol on a multi-
condition lower-limb biomechanics dataset, the proposed archi-
tecture achieves r = 0.706 ± 0.139 and R² = 0.474 ± 0.208
without subject-specific adaptation. With only 0.5% adaptation
data, performance increases to r = 0.761 ± 0.030 and R² = 0.559
± 0.047, demonstrating rapid adaptation and early performance
saturation. These results support attention-based architectures
combined with lightweight adaptation as a practical and scalable
alternative to direct EMG sensing for real-world wearable robotic
applications.
Index Terms—Wearable robotics, inertial measurement units
(IMUs), electromyography (EMG), human-robot interaction.
I. INTRODUCTION
H
UMAN–robot interaction (HRI) systems, including up-
per and lower-limb exoskeletons, powered prostheses,
and assistive robots, heavily rely on the estimation of neu-
romuscular activity to enable natural, safe, and personalised
control [1]. Access to muscle activation patterns enables
adaptive assistance, enhances safety, and supports subject-
specific control strategies aligned with individual motor capa-
bilities [2]. However, direct electromyography (EMG) acqui-
sition remains difficult to deploy reliably outside laboratory
environments. EMG signals are highly sensitive to electrode
placement, motion artifacts, and long-term instability, and
exhibit substantial inter- and intra-subject variability in clinical
populations, particularly [3]. These limitations significantly
inhibit the scalability and long-term usability of EMG-driven
interfaces in wearable robotic systems. On the other hand,
Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) provide a practical al-
ternative for biomechanical estimation in ecological settings.
IMUs enable robust measurement of kinematic and spatiotem-
poral motion parameters without laboratory infrastructure [4].
Recent learning-based approaches have demonstrated that in-
ertial signals can be leveraged to infer joint kinetics and

even muscle activation patterns from kinematics alone [5],
[6]. However, most existing methods rely on static models
trained offline on multi-subject datasets, implicitly assuming
that inter-subject variability can be absorbed during training. In
practice, neuromuscular activation strategies remain strongly
individualized. As a result, performance often degrades when
these predictors are deployed on unseen users, limiting their
translational potential. In contrast, adaptive control is a founda-
tional principle in robotics, routinely employed to compensate
for model uncertainty and subject variability [7]. Controllers
update internal parameters to preserve stability and perfor-
mance under changing conditions. Despite this paradigm,
adaptive mechanisms remain largely absent in learning-based
neuromuscular estimation, where neural models are typically
treated as fixed after offline training [8], [9]. Additionally,
the validation procedures of these methods often consider
simplified scenarios only (e.g., during level-ground walking)
without taking into account the variability of real-world en-
vironments. This disconnect becomes particularly critical in
wearable robotics, where subject-specific neuromuscular dy-
namics and environmental complexity (e.g., stair negotiation,
walking on inclined surfaces), directly affect the effectiveness
and safety of assistance [10]. In this work, we propose an
adaptive learning framework for IMU-based muscle activity
estimation. The proposed system combines a neural architec-
ture explicitly designed to enhance cross-subject generalization
with a lightweight adaptation mechanism that enables fast
personalization to previously unseen users. The proposed
method is validated on a gait-related lower-limb dataset,
demonstrating its efficacy across diverse locomotion scenarios
(level ground, stairs, slopes, and treadmill walking). The
contributions of this work are threefold. First, we introduce
a novel neural architecture for cross-subject neuromuscular
estimation from wearable inertial sensing, achieving state-of-
the-art performance in level-ground walking while maintaining
transferability across users. Second, we systematically evaluate
the model across multiple locomotion modes, demonstrating
improved robustness to task and environmental variability
relevant to real-world robotic deployment. Third, we show that
a lightweight subject-specific adaptation requires only a few
steps to yield consistent performance gains across conditions,
enabling practical personalization within an adaptive robotics
framework.

II. RELATED WORK
EMG has been widely investigated as a physiological in-
terface for motion intention recognition and torque estimation
in wearable robotics. Recurrent neural networks, particularly
Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architectures, have demon-
strated accurate prediction of joint torques and kinematics
from EMG signals in both intra and inter-subject settings
[11]. Similarly, deep sequence models have been employed to
estimate joint angles and moments from multi-muscle EMG
recordings during daily activities [12]. Beyond purely data-
driven approaches, EMG-driven musculoskeletal models have
enabled real-time estimation of joint moments and spinal
loading during assistive tasks [13]. Deep learning has also been
integrated within exoskeleton control loops, where EMG-based
predictions are coupled with impedance controllers to improve
synchronization [14]. Despite these advances, EMG-based
systems remain limited by signal non-stationarity, electrode
placement sensitivity, and strong subject dependence [15],
[16]. Recent benchmarking efforts further highlight limited
out-of-distribution generalization in real-world scenarios [17].
Crucially, most learning-based EMG estimators depend on
subject-specific calibration or fine-tuning after offline training
[18], [19]. While such personalization enhances accuracy, it
typically demands quantitative subject-specific data, constrain-
ing scalability and imposing significant deployment overhead
in real-world wearable robotic systems. IMUs provide a
portable alternative to laboratory motion capture for biome-
chanical analysis. Convolutional and recurrent architectures
have demonstrated accurate prediction of joint kinematics from
wearable inertial sensors in subject-independent settings [20].
Transfer learning strategies have been proposed to improve
personalization when limited subject-specific data are available
[21]. Recent works have extended IMU-based learning to the
estimation of joint moments and ground reaction forces across
multiple locomotion conditions [6], [22]. These approaches
show promising cross-subject generalization in offline evalu-
ations. However, adaptation to new users is typically handled
via post hoc fine-tuning or complete subject-specific retrain-
ing approaches that generally rely on non-trivial amounts of
subject-specific data. Systematic investigation of structured,
rapid initial adaptation strategies, compatible with real-world
deployment constraints, remains limited. Adaptive control
strategies have been widely adopted in wearable robotics to
achieve subject-specific assistance through impedance modu-
lation and interaction-force feedback within assist-as-needed
paradigms [23]. Extensions toward dynamic synchronization
and task-dependent trajectory adaptation have been proposed
using adaptive movement primitives and interaction-aware
controllers [24]. Human-in-the-loop control frameworks fur-
ther integrate stability constraints and ergonomic objectives
to improve robustness across different environmental condi-
tions [25]. Data-driven personalization has increasingly been
explored to reduce reliance on explicit human–robot modeling.
Reinforcement learning has been applied to optimize assistive
torque profiles and timing parameters [26], while Bayesian
optimization and neural trajectory translators have been incor-
porated for multi-task generalization [27]. Although effective,
these approaches typically require iterative interaction cycles
or extended adaptation phases. To reduce calibration effort,
meta-learning and few-shot transfer strategies have recently
emerged. Model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) has been
used to personalize myoelectric upper-limb exoskeleton con-
trol with short calibration sequences [28]. Similarly, Reptile-
based few-shot transfer learning has been investigated for
wearable IMU-based human activity recognition (HAR) under
limited labeled data [29], and broader surveys highlight gen-
eralization challenges in IMU-based HAR [30]. Despite these
advances, existing methods predominantly focus on trajectory
generation, torque tuning, motion classification, or activity
recognition, rather than continuous neuromuscular regression
under strict data-efficiency and deployment constraints.
III. METHODOLOGY
The overall method is summarized in Fig. 1, and it is
composed of three main blocks: Signal Processing, GEGLU-
Transformer, and Few-Shot Adaptation. The methodology was
evaluated on a gait dataset [31], enabling direct comparison
with existing approaches in the locomotion literature. Al-
though the experimental validation focuses on gait data, the
problem formulation and the proposed architecture are task-
agnostic. The framework operates on synchronized kinematic
and myoelectric time series and does not embed gait-specific
assumptions. Therefore, it can be directly extended to upper-
limb movements or other robotic and assistive scenarios.

B. Signal Processing
Before being used for model training, raw EMG and IMU
signals need to be pre-processed. Therefore, we used the same
pipeline described in [8], ensuring methodological consistency
with prior IMU-to-EMG estimation frameworks and standard
electrophysiological practices.
a) EMG Processing: Surface EMG signals are processed
according to the recommendations of the International Society
of Electrophysiology and Kinesiology (ISEK) standards [32].
Signals are sampled at 1000 Hz and band-pass filtered using
a fourth-order Butterworth filter (20–450 Hz) to attenuate
motion artifacts and high-frequency noise. The filtered signals
are then full-wave rectified and subsequently low-pass filtered
at 8 Hz using a fourth-order Butterworth filter to extract
smooth muscle activation envelopes suitable for regression
modeling.
b) Temporal Alignment and Resampling: IMU signals
are sampled at 200 Hz. EMG envelopes are temporally aligned
with IMU signals and resampled to 200 Hz via linear inter-
polation to ensure synchronized input–target pairs.
c) Movement Segmentation: The dataset is segmented
into a set of stand-alone movement sequences. In the used
walking dataset, heel-strike events are employed to segment
the data into individual gait cycles. Each cycle is time-
normalized to 101 samples representing 0–100% of the gait
cycle. This normalization enables consistent temporal model-
ing across subjects and walking conditions.
d) Post-Segmentation Filtering: After time normaliza-
tion, segmented IMU and EMG signals were median-filtered to
attenuate residual impulsive artifacts and independently scaled
to [0, 1] via min–max normalization.
C. Gaussian Error Gated Linear Unit Transformer
The proposed architecture builds upon the Transformer
encoder framework originally introduced in [33]. Compared
to recurrent models, Transformers enable parallel sequence
processing while preserving global temporal context through
multi-head attention. An overview of the complete processing
and modeling pipeline is illustrated in Fig. 1, where the bottom
panel presents the proposed GEGLU-Transformer architecture,
composed of a temporal convolutional embedding layer, po-
sitional encoding, four stacked self-attention encoder layers,
and a final linear projection head for multi-muscle EMG pre-
diction. Each encoder layer follows the standard Transformer
structure with residual connections and layer normalization, as
shown in Fig. 2. The self-attention block enables the model to
capture long-range temporal dependencies across multimodal
sensor inputs.
a) Convolutional Front-End: Given the high temporal
resolution and multi-channel structure of IMU signals, a 1D
convolutional front-end is first applied to extract local motion
patterns prior to attention-based modeling. Convolutional pre-
processing has been shown to improve stability and inductive
bias in time-series Transformers. Specifically, a Conv1D layer
(kernel size 5) projects the 24 inertial features into a 256-
dimensional latent space. Group Normalization is employed
to enhance robustness under moderate batch sizes, followed
by Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELU) activations, which
have become standard in Transformer-based architectures.
b) Self-Attention Encoder: Temporal dependencies are
modeled through a stack of four Transformer encoder layers
with multi-head self-attention (8 heads). A Pre-Norm con-
figuration is adopted, where Layer Normalization is applied
before both the attention and feed-forward blocks, improving
optimization stability in deep Transformers. Dropout regular-
ization is applied after both the attention and feed-forward
sublayers to improve generalization.

D. Few-shot Adaptation
Given a small adaptation set Dada composed of movement
segments from an unseen test subject, the model parameters
are adapted by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE)
loss defined in Eq. (2). All parameters are updated (i.e., no
layer freezing is applied), enabling full-network personaliza-
tion to subject-specific neuromuscular patterns. Adaptation is
performed under strict data and computational constraints to
mitigate catastrophic forgetting and ensure numerical stability.
IV. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
A. Dataset
The proposed framework was evaluated using the publicly
available lower-limb biomechanics dataset [31]. The dataset
comprises synchronized inertial measurements and surface
electromyography recordings collected from 22 healthy adults
during multiple locomotion tasks. Each participant was in-
strumented with four wearable IMUs placed on the lower
limbs, providing tri-axial accelerometer and gyroscope signals
sampled at 200 Hz. Surface EMG was recorded from eleven
lower-limb muscles at 1000 Hz using bipolar electrodes. Out
of the eleven recorded muscles, ten lower-limb muscles were
considered in this work: gastrocnemius medialis, tibialis ante-
rior, soleus, vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, rectus femoris,
biceps femoris, semitendinosus, gracilis, and gluteus medius.
The right external oblique was excluded from the analysis,
as it is not directly involved in lower-limb actuation and was
outside the scope of the proposed neuromuscular modeling
framework. The dataset includes treadmill walking at multiple
speeds, level-ground walking, stair ascent/descent, and ramp
ascent/descent. For this study, only IMU signals were used as
model inputs, while processed EMG envelopes were used as
ground-truth neuromuscular targets.
B. Experimental Protocol
A leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation scheme
was adopted to evaluate the proposed method. For each fold,
one subject was held out for testing, while the remaining
subjects were used for training. The base model was trained
offline using only training-subject data. Model selection and
hyperparameter tuning were performed exclusively on a vali-
dation subset extracted from the training pool, ensuring strict
subject independence and preventing data leakage. To evaluate
the effectiveness of the proposed approach, we compared with
two state-of-the-art models that have already being used for
IMU-to-EMG estimation in walking task. We first reproduced
the LSTM-based estimator proposed in [8], followed by its
CNN-LSTM extension introduced in [9]. The CNN-LSTM
architecture was further refined by replacing the original
2D convolutional processing (which treated the input as a
time–feature image) with 1D temporal convolutions, preserv-
ing the sequential structure of inertial signals prior to recurrent
modeling. Batch normalization and deeper LSTM layers with
dropout were introduced to improve optimization stability and
temporal representation capacity. In their original works, both
the baseline methods considered only level-ground walking
conditions, excluding the other walking tasks. Thus, an ini-
tial benchmarking phase was conducted using level-ground
walking data only, for both training and testing. This stage
allows a fair comparison with prior IMU-to-EMG approaches
and isolates architectural differences without the confounding
effect of multiple locomotion modes. After completing the
level-ground benchmarking phase, all models were retrained
from scratch using the full multi-condition dataset, including
level-ground, stair ascent/descent, ramp walking, and treadmill
locomotion.
C. Training
The proposed model, as well as the state-of-the-art base-
line models, were optimized using stochastic gradient-based
methods. The LSTM and CNN–LSTM architectures were
trained with the Adam optimizer using a learning rate of 10−3,
whereas the GEGLU-Transformer model employed AdamW
with a learning rate of 3 × 10−4 and weight decay of 10−2
to improve regularization of the attention-based architecture.
MSE was adopted as the regression objective for all models.
Within each LOSO fold, data from the training subjects were
randomly partitioned into 80% training and 20% validation
subsets. The held-out test subject was strictly excluded from all
stages of offline optimization, including model selection and
hyperparameter tuning. Models were trained for a maximum
of 1000 epochs using mini-batches of size 128. Early stopping
with a patience of 50 epochs was applied based on validation
loss, and the model achieving the lowest validation error was
retained for deployment. All experiments were implemented
in PyTorch and executed on a GPU-enabled high-performance
computing cluster equipped with NVIDIA RTX GPUs.


D. Deployment
At deployment, the trained models were evaluated on unseen
subjects. As explained in Section III-D, a few-shot adaptation
strategy was applied, where a small fraction of subject-specific
gait cycles was used for initial calibration. Calibration ratios
of 0.5%, 1%, 2%, 5%, and 10% of the test set were evaluated
under the LOSO protocol. Across folds, these percentages
correspond on average to approximately 10, 22, 46, 120, and
241 gait cycles, respectively, out of ∼2400 test cycles per
subject. During subject-specific calibration, model parameters
were updated using a reduced learning rate of 5 × 10−5.
Adam was used for the CNN and CNN–LSTM models, while
AdamW was adopted for the GEGLU-Transformer archi-
tecture to maintain consistency with its offline optimization
scheme. For each calibration phase, 40 gradient update steps
were performed over the selected subject-specific gait cycles.
All network parameters were updated (no layer freezing), and
gradient norm clipping with threshold 1.0 was applied to
enhance numerical stability during adaptation.
E. Metrics
Model performance was evaluated using complementary
accuracy and physiological consistency metrics. Standard re-
gression measures included normalized root mean square error
(nRMSE), Pearson correlation coefficient (r), and coefficient
of determination (R2), assessing overall reconstruction fidelity
and temporal similarity between predicted and ground-truth
EMG envelopes. Peak timing error (∆Tp) was computed as

A. Impact of GEGLU Gating
We evaluated the impact of replacing the standard feed-
forward block with a GEGLU-gated formulation. Although
improvements are moderate in absolute terms, they are consis-
tent across metrics. GEGLU yields a relative gain of +0.33%
in correlation (r), +1.52% in R2, and a −0.65% reduction in
nRMSE compared to the non-gated Transformer. Peak-related
metrics, however, do not improve and remain comparable to
the non-gated variants. Importantly, performance variability is
slightly reduced, indicating improved cross-subject stability.
Given the negligible increase in architectural complexity and
the systematic improvement across evaluation metrics, we
adopt GEGLU in the final model as a more robust feed-
forward formulation.

these results highlight the superior sample efficiency of the

VI. DISCUSSION
The experimental results highlight three main findings.
First, the proposed GEGLU-Transformer consistently im-
proves cross-subject generalization compared to the baselines,
both when considering all locomotion modalities jointly and
when restricting the analysis to level-ground only. This indi-
cates that the performance gain is not condition-specific but
reflects a more robust subject-invariant representation. This
suggests that self-attention mechanisms are more effective in
modeling long-range temporal dependencies in neuromuscular
signals, while gated feed-forward modulation enhances feature
selectivity and stability. Second, the advantage becomes par-
ticularly evident in amplitude-related metrics. The reduction in
peak estimation errors indicates that the model better captures
activation magnitude, not only temporal alignment. This is
especially relevant for applications involving assistive control
or torque estimation, where amplitude fidelity directly impacts
actuation accuracy. Third, the online adaptation analysis re-
veals a markedly faster personalization dynamic. The GEGLU-
Transformer reaches near-plateau performance with minimal
calibration data, indicating that the learned representation
is well-structured and easily fine-tuned. In practical robotic
settings, this reduces calibration time and increases usability in
real-world deployments. Performance differences across mus-
cles further suggest that high-amplitude and more regularly
patterned muscles (e.g., plantarflexors and vasti) benefit most
from the proposed architecture, whereas biarticular or low-
activation muscles remain challenging for all models. This
indicates that part of the prediction difficulty may stem from
signal quality and biomechanical variability rather than model
capacity alone. These findings suggest that self-attention with
gated feed-forward modulation enables stronger global model-
ing and more efficient adaptation than recurrent approaches.
VII. CONCLUSION
This work introduces a GEGLU-Transformer architecture
for cross-subject neuromuscular signal reconstruction and few-
shot adaptation. Under the LOSO protocol, the proposed
model consistently outperformed recurrent baselines across all
evaluation metrics, demonstrating improved waveform sim-
ilarity, reduced amplitude and timing errors, and stronger
generalization to unseen subjects. Notably, these improve-
ments were observed both across mixed locomotion modalities
and under level-ground-only evaluation, confirming condition-
independent robustness. In addition, the GEGLU-Transformer
exhibited significantly faster adaptation. Substantial perfor-
mance gains were achieved with as little adaptation data, and
performance rapidly approached a plateau, indicating efficient
subject-specific personalization. This behavior suggests that
the proposed adaptation framework is methodologically gen-
eral and can extend beyond lower-limb locomotion to other


human movements, including upper-limb tasks. However, the
dataset includes fixed stair geometries and incline levels,
potentially limiting generalization to different environmen-
tal configurations. Future work will investigate robustness
to varying terrain geometries and continuous adaptation in
dynamically changing real-world environments.

Abstract: Reliable estimation of neuromuscular activation is a key enabler for adaptive and personalized control in wearable robotics. However, surface electromyography (EMG) remains difficult to deploy robustly outside laboratory settings due to electrode sensitivity, signal non-stationarity, and strong subject dependence. In this work, we propose an adaptive IMU-to- EMG learning framework that reconstructs continuous muscle activation envelopes from wearable inertial measurements across heterogeneous movement conditions. The approach combines a Transformer encoder with Gaussian Error Gated Linear Units (GEGLU-Transformer) to enhance cross-subject general- ization and enable rapid subject-specific personalization. Un- der a strict leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocol on a multi- condition lower-limb biomechanics dataset, the proposed archi- tecture achieves r = 0.706 ± 0.139 and R² = 0.474 ± 0.208 without subject-specific adaptation. With only 0.5% adaptation data, performance increases to r = 0.761 ± 0.030 and R² = 0.559 ± 0.047, demonstrating rapid adaptation and early performance saturation. These results support attention-based architectures combined with lightweight adaptation as a practical and scalable alternative to direct EMG sensing for real-world wearable robotic applications.
